$comment: Plain-language explanations for Python / Django / Flask findings (bot/lib/adapters/python.ts). Keyed by finding kind. See common.json for the format. Facts checked against docs.python.org What's New 3.12-3.14, PEP 594/632, the Flask and Werkzeug changelogs and the Django deprecation timeline on 2026-11-13.

codemod.pyupgrade.inPlainWords: pyupgrade rewrites old-style code into the form current Python prefers. It doesn't change what the code does.
codemod.pyupgrade.whatWeFound: {count} file(s) still use older syntax, such as typing.List, super(Class, self), u"" strings, .format() or class X(object).
codemod.pyupgrade.whyItMatters: The old forms still run, but they're noise in every review and some (typing.List and friends) are deprecated. Cleaning them now keeps later upgrades small.
codemod.pyupgrade.whatWillHappen: pyupgrade {flag} runs on every unlocked .py file. Its changes are committed on their own so you can review them.
codemod.pyupgrade.ifApproved: The code uses modern syntax; behaviour stays the same.
codemod.pyupgrade.ifLocked: Locked files keep the old syntax. That's fine: Python {targetPython} still runs it, so nothing breaks. The rest of the project is still rewritten.
manualSteps: Run pyupgrade {flag} on the locked files later, when you're ready.
Review the diff for files you care about.

codemod.django-upgrade.inPlainWords: django-upgrade rewrites Django calls that were removed or renamed, so the code works on Django {django}.
codemod.django-upgrade.whatWeFound: The project uses Django {fromDjango}. {count} file(s) use APIs that django-upgrade rewrites.
codemod.django-upgrade.whyItMatters: Django removes deprecated APIs on a fixed schedule. Calls like force_text, ugettext and url() no longer exist in Django 4.0+, so imports fail and the app won't start.
codemod.django-upgrade.whatWillHappen: django-upgrade {flag} runs on every unlocked .py file. Every change is committed so you can review it.
codemod.django-upgrade.ifApproved: The code matches Django {django} and the tests run against it.
codemod.django-upgrade.ifLocked: Locked files keep the removed Django calls while the app runs on Django {django}. Importing them fails with ImportError, so the Test step fails.
manualSteps: Rewrite each removed call listed below by hand (see the deprecation timeline).
Run the tests that import those modules.

django-api.codemod.inPlainWords: This line uses {api}, which Django {removedIn} removed. django-upgrade changes it to {replacement}.
django-api.codemod.whyItMatters: On Django {django} the name no longer exists, so importing this module fails and every view or test that touches it breaks.
django-api.codemod.ifApproved: The line is rewritten and behaves the same on Django {django}.
django-api.codemod.ifLocked: Locking keeps the whole file ({file}) unchanged, so the removed call stays. On Django {django} the import fails and the Test step fails.
manualSteps: Replace {api} with {replacement}.
Run the tests for this module.

rules.requirements.inPlainWords: The pinned versions of the framework and test tools are raised to releases that support Python {targetPython}.
rules.requirements.whyItMatters: Old pins often don't work on a new Python. For example, pytest 7.0 crashes on Python 3.14 (it uses ast.Str, which 3.14 removed) and Flask 2.0 lacks fixes for current Werkzeug. This is the upgrade itself.
rules.requirements.whatWillHappen: Each pin shown below is raised (exact pins stay exact). pip installs the new versions into a fresh venv before the tests run.
rules.requirements.ifApproved: The tests run against the new versions.
rules.requirements.ifLocked: {fileName} keeps the old pins, so pip installs the old releases on Python {targetPython}. They crash or fail to install, and the Test step fails.
manualSteps: Raise the pins shown below by hand.
Create a venv on Python {targetPython}, pip install, and run the tests.

rules.pyproject.inPlainWords: The project's packaging metadata says which Python it needs. It's raised to {targetPython}.
rules.pyproject.whyItMatters: requires-python (or python_requires) is what pip and your users read. If it still says an old version, the upgrade isn't recorded and the old Python can still be used.
rules.pyproject.whatWillHappen: The version range is set to the target, as shown below.
rules.pyproject.ifApproved: The metadata says Python {targetPython} and the checks confirm it.
rules.pyproject.ifLocked: {fileName} keeps the old Python range. The code may run fine, but the Checks step sees the old declaration and fails the run.
manualSteps: Set requires-python (or python_requires) to >={targetPython} by hand.

learnMore.label: Dropping support for older Python versions

rules.python-version.inPlainWords: The file that tells pyenv, uv or your host which Python to use is updated.
rules.python-version.whyItMatters: Developers' tools and some hosting platforms pick the interpreter from this file.
rules.python-version.whatWillHappen: The version in {fileName} is set to {targetPython} (runtime.txt gets the newest patch release).
rules.python-version.ifApproved: Everyone using the file switches to Python {targetPython}.
rules.python-version.ifLocked: The dry run isn't affected, but developers and the hosting platform keep using the old Python.
manualSteps: Put {targetPython} in {fileName}.

rules.stdlib.plainTitle: Replace standard-library calls Python removed ({count} change(s) in {fileName})
rules.stdlib.inPlainWords: Some old standard-library names were deleted in Python 3.12. The rules swap them for the official replacements.
rules.stdlib.whyItMatters: Removed names fail the moment they run: assertEquals raises AttributeError, import imp raises ModuleNotFoundError, and SafeConfigParser no longer exists.
rules.stdlib.whatWillHappen: Each line is rewritten exactly as shown below (assertEquals → assertEqual, SafeConfigParser → ConfigParser, readfp → read_file, imp.reload → importlib.reload).
rules.stdlib.ifLocked: {fileName} keeps the removed calls. On Python {targetPython} they raise AttributeError or ModuleNotFoundError, so the Test step fails.
manualSteps: Apply the replacements shown below by hand.
Run the tests on Python {targetPython}.

rules.flask-imports.plainTitle: Import Markup and escape from markupsafe ({fileName})
rules.flask-imports.inPlainWords: Flask 3 no longer re-exports Markup and escape. They now come straight from markupsafe, which Flask already depends on.
rules.flask-imports.whyItMatters: On Flask {flask} the line `from flask import Markup` raises ImportError, so the whole module (and the app) fails to load.
rules.flask-imports.whatWillHappen: The import is split: Markup and escape come from markupsafe, the other names stay on flask, as shown below.
rules.flask-imports.ifApproved: The module loads on Flask {flask}; HTML escaping behaves the same.
rules.flask-imports.ifLocked: {fileName} keeps `from flask import Markup/escape`. On Flask {flask} that's an ImportError, so the app can't start and the Test step fails.
manualSteps: Change the import to `from markupsafe import Markup, escape`.
Run the tests.

rules.flask-json-config.inPlainWords: Flask 2.3 removed the JSON_* config keys. The same settings now live on app.json.
rules.flask-json-config.whyItMatters: Setting a removed key doesn't raise an error. Flask silently ignores it, so responses change (for example, keys get sorted again) without any warning.
rules.flask-json-config.whatWillHappen: The line is rewritten to set the matching app.json attribute, as shown below.
rules.flask-json-config.ifApproved: JSON responses keep the behaviour the old setting asked for.
rules.flask-json-config.ifLocked: The old config line stays and is silently ignored on Flask {flask}. Tests usually still pass, but API responses can change (key order, ASCII escaping, mimetype).
manualSteps: Replace app.config["JSON_…"] with the app.json attribute shown below.
Check one JSON response by hand.

install.venv.plainTitle: Install the new versions into a fresh Python {python} venv
install.venv.inPlainWords: pip installs the upgraded packages into a throwaway virtual environment, so the tests run against them.
install.venv.whyItMatters: Without installing, the tests would still run old packages and prove nothing.
install.venv.whatWillHappen: A venv is created outside the project (in the run's own folder) and pip installs the dependencies. Nothing is installed into the project or into your system Python.
install.venv.ifApproved: Dependencies are installed with the new versions.
install.venv.ifLocked: This is project-wide and can't be locked. Marking it manual only adds a note to the report; the install still runs because the tests need it.
manualSteps: After merging, recreate your own venv on Python {python} and reinstall.

install.none.plainTitle: No dependency list pip can install
install.none.inPlainWords: The tool installs Python projects with pip, and this project has no file pip can read.
install.none.whatWeFound: The project has no requirements*.txt, no [project] table in pyproject.toml and no setup.py.
install.none.whyItMatters: Preflight refuses the run: there would be nothing to test against.
install.none.whatWillHappen: Nothing; the run stops at Preflight.
manualSteps: Export a requirements.txt (for example: pipenv requirements > requirements.txt), or add a [project] table to pyproject.toml.
Plan again.

python-module.removed.plainTitle: The {api} no longer exists in Python {removedIn}+
python-module.removed.inPlainWords: This line imports a standard-library module that Python deleted, so the import fails on Python {targetPython}.
python-module.removed.whyItMatters: A missing module fails with ModuleNotFoundError as soon as the file is imported, which usually takes the whole app down with it.
python-module.removed.whatWillHappen: No rewrite tool replaces whole modules. If a test fails, the AI fix-up may port it to {replacement}.
python-module.removed.ifApproved: Tests that import this file fail; the AI fix-up gets a few tries.
python-module.removed.ifLocked: The AI fix-up can't touch the file, so the import stays and fails on Python {targetPython}. The Test step fails.
manualSteps: Replace the module with {replacement}.
Run the code path that uses it.

python-api.removed.inPlainWords: This line calls a standard-library function or class that Python deleted.
python-api.removed.whyItMatters: The call raises AttributeError or ImportError on Python {targetPython}, so the feature using it breaks.
python-api.removed.whatWillHappen: No rule rewrites this one safely. If a test fails, the AI fix-up may replace it with {replacement}.
python-api.removed.ifApproved: Tests that reach this line fail; the AI fix-up gets a few tries.
python-api.removed.ifLocked: The AI fix-up can't touch the file, so the call stays and fails on Python {targetPython}.
manualSteps: Replace {api} with {replacement}.
Run the code path that uses it.

python-api.deprecated.inPlainWords: This still works on Python {targetPython} but prints a DeprecationWarning and will be removed in a later version.
python-api.deprecated.whyItMatters: Nothing breaks today. It becomes an error in a future Python, and warnings in the test output hide real problems.
python-api.deprecated.whatWillHappen: Nothing is changed automatically. The report lists it as a follow-up.
python-api.deprecated.ifApproved: The run passes; the warning stays until someone replaces it.
python-api.deprecated.ifLocked: Same as approving: the call stays and keeps warning.
manualSteps: Replace {api} with {replacement}.
Check the result is still the same (for utcnow, the new value is timezone-aware).

flask-api.removed.inPlainWords: This line uses a Flask feature that no longer exists in Flask {flask}.
flask-api.removed.whyItMatters: On Flask {flask} the name is gone: the app fails to start (AttributeError / ImportError) or the setting is silently ignored.
flask-api.removed.whatWillHappen: No rule rewrites this one safely (it needs a small redesign). If a test fails, the AI fix-up may port it to {replacement}.
flask-api.removed.ifApproved: Tests that load this code fail; the AI fix-up gets a few tries.
flask-api.removed.ifLocked: The AI fix-up can't touch the file, so the removed API stays and the app fails on Flask {flask}.
manualSteps: Port it to {replacement}.
Run the tests and start the app once.

flask-api.deprecated.inPlainWords: This still works on Flask {flask} but warns, and Flask plans to remove it.
flask-api.deprecated.whyItMatters: Nothing breaks today, but the next Flask release can remove it.
flask-api.deprecated.whatWillHappen: Nothing is changed automatically. The report lists it as a follow-up.
flask-api.deprecated.ifApproved: The run passes; the DeprecationWarning stays.
flask-api.deprecated.ifLocked: Same as approving: the line stays and keeps warning.
manualSteps: Use {replacement} instead.

werkzeug-api.removed.inPlainWords: Flask {flask} needs Werkzeug 3, which deleted these URL helpers.
werkzeug-api.removed.whyItMatters: The import fails with ImportError as soon as the module loads.
werkzeug-api.removed.whatWillHappen: Nothing is rewritten automatically. If a test fails, the AI fix-up may switch to {replacement}.
werkzeug-api.removed.ifApproved: Tests that import this file fail; the AI fix-up gets a few tries.
werkzeug-api.removed.ifLocked: The AI fix-up can't touch the file, so the import stays and fails.
manualSteps: Use {replacement} from the standard library instead.
Run the tests.

django-api.removed.inPlainWords: This line uses a Django API that django-upgrade can't rewrite for you.
django-api.removed.whyItMatters: On Django {django} the name is gone, so the module fails to import.
django-api.removed.whatWillHappen: Nothing is rewritten automatically. If a test fails, the AI fix-up may port it to {replacement}.
django-api.removed.ifApproved: Tests that import this file fail; the AI fix-up gets a few tries.
django-api.removed.ifLocked: The AI fix-up can't touch the file, so the removed API stays and the import fails.
manualSteps: Port it to {replacement}.
Run the tests for this app.

learnMore.label: Django: upgrading to a newer version

django.default-auto-field.inPlainWords: Django wants you to say which column type automatic ids use. This project doesn't say yet.
django.default-auto-field.whyItMatters: Django warns about every model (models.W042). If someone later picks BigAutoField without care, makemigrations alters every primary key in the database.
django.default-auto-field.ifApproved: The run passes with warnings; the setting is still missing.
django.default-auto-field.ifLocked: Same as approving: nothing changes, the warnings stay.
manualSteps: Add DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD = "django.db.models.AutoField" to keep today's id columns.
Run python manage.py makemigrations --check to confirm nothing changes.

django.use-tz.plainTitle: USE_TZ turns on by default in Django 5.0
django.use-tz.inPlainWords: Django 5.0 changed a default: datetimes become timezone-aware unless the settings say otherwise.
django.use-tz.whatWeFound: {file} doesn't set USE_TZ, so it relies on the old default (False).
django.use-tz.whyItMatters: After the upgrade, stored and displayed times can shift and comparisons between naive and aware datetimes raise TypeError at runtime.
django.use-tz.ifApproved: The run may pass while times behave differently in production.
django.use-tz.ifLocked: Same as approving: the default still changes.
manualSteps: Add USE_TZ = False to keep today's behaviour, or plan the move to aware datetimes.
Check views and reports that show dates.

dependency.pydantic-v1.inPlainWords: pydantic 2 changed how models work, and this route doesn't make that jump for you.
dependency.pydantic-v1.whyItMatters: pydantic 1.x has no builds for current Python lines, so pip install fails, and moving to v2 changes model code.
dependency.pydantic-v1.ifApproved: pip install will likely fail at the Test step.
dependency.pydantic-v1.ifLocked: Same as approving: the old pin stays and pip install fails.
manualSteps: Migrate to pydantic v2 first (the bump-pydantic tool helps).
Plan this migration again.

dependency.native-wheel.inPlainWords: {name} contains compiled code. An old pin may have no ready-made download (wheel) for Python {python}.
dependency.native-wheel.whyItMatters: Without a wheel, pip tries to compile it from source. That needs a C compiler and usually fails, especially on Windows.
dependency.native-wheel.whatWillHappen: This pin is not bumped by the route.
dependency.native-wheel.ifApproved: pip install may fail at the Test step; the AI fix-up may raise the pin.
dependency.native-wheel.ifLocked: The pin stays as is, and so does the risk.
manualSteps: Check PyPI for a {name} release with Python {python} wheels.
Raise the pin and run the tests.

dependency.manual.plainTitle: A dependency the rules can't update
dependency.manual.inPlainWords: This dependency comes from a URL, a git repository or a local path, so the rules can't set its version.
dependency.manual.whyItMatters: If that source has no release for the new Python or framework, pip install fails.
dependency.manual.whatWillHappen: The line is left exactly as it is.
dependency.manual.ifApproved: It's left alone; check it after the run.
manualSteps: Point it at a release that supports Python {targetPython}.
Run pip install and the tests.

tests.pytest-undeclared.plainTitle: The tests need pytest, but it isn't listed
tests.pytest-undeclared.inPlainWords: Some tests import pytest, but no dependency file mentions it, so the fresh venv won't have it.
tests.pytest-undeclared.whatWeFound: Test files import pytest; no requirements file, extra or group declares it.
tests.pytest-undeclared.whyItMatters: The test run fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest' before any test runs.
tests.pytest-undeclared.ifApproved: The Test step will likely fail.
manualSteps: Add pytest to requirements-dev.txt (or a test extra).
Plan again.

package-manager.python.inPlainWords: This project uses {manager}. The run installs with pip, so the {manager} lockfile keeps the old versions.
package-manager.python.whyItMatters: Teammates and CI that install from the lockfile keep getting the old versions until it's regenerated.
package-manager.python.whatWillHappen: The run edits the dependency declarations and tests with pip. {lockfile} is left alone.
package-manager.python.ifApproved: The run proceeds; re-lock after merging.
package-manager.python.ifLocked: Same: the lockfile is never edited.
manualSteps: Re-lock with {manager} after the migration.
Commit the new lockfile in the same pull request.
